title: The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
summary: This chapter traces how the idea of the nation state took root in Europe after the French Revolution of 1789. Frédéric Sorrieu's 1848 prints visualised a world of democratic and social republics, while the French Revolution itself created citizens, the tricolour, the Marseillaise and a centralised national identity. Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 spread equality before law and the right to property across Europe, though at the cost of taxation, conscription and censorship. Liberal nationalism demanded constitutions and free markets, expressed economically through the Prussian-led Zollverein of 1834. The conservative order restored at the Congress of Vienna in 1815 under Metternich tried to suppress these currents, driving revolutionaries like Mazzini into secret societies. Revolutions of 1830 and 1848 swept France, Belgium, Greece and Germany, where the Frankfurt Parliament failed. Culture, romanticism, folklore and language, especially in Poland, nourished national feeling. Finally the chapter explains the unification of Germany under Bismarck and of Italy through Cavour and Garibaldi, the gradual making of Britain, the allegories Marianne and Germania, and the Balkan rivalries that exploded into the First World War.
hotTopics: Sorrieu's prints of 1848 and the utopian vision
French Revolution and creation of national identity
Napoleonic Code of 1804 and its impact
Congress of Vienna 1815 and conservative order
Romanticism, Herder and language based nationalism
The Balkan crisis and the First World War

sections.heading: Frédéric Sorrieu and the Dream of a World of Republics
sections.para: In 1848, Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, prepared a series of four prints visualising his dream of a world made up of democratic and social republics. The first print shows the peoples of Europe and America marching in a long train and offering homage to the Statue of Liberty as they pass by it. Liberty personified carries the torch of Enlightenment in one hand and the Charter of the Rights of Man in the other. On the ground in the foreground lie the shattered remains of the symbols of absolutist institutions. The United States and Switzerland, which were by then already nation states, lead the procession, while the peoples of Germany, France, Austria and other lands follow behind, identified through their flags and national costumes. From the heavens above, Christ, saints and angels gaze upon the scene, symbolising the fraternity of nations. Sorrieu called this utopian vision the United States of the World. Remember: absolutist means a monarchical government that was unrestrained by any constitution, and utopian means a vision of a society that is so ideal that it is unlikely to actually exist.
points: Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, made a series of four prints in 1848 visualising his dream of a world made of democratic and social republics.
The first print shows the peoples of Europe and America marching past the Statue of Liberty, which holds the torch of Enlightenment and the Charter of the Rights of Man.
The shattered remains of absolutist institutions lie in the foreground of the print, symbolising the end of unrestrained monarchies.
The United States and Switzerland, already nation states by 1848, lead the procession of peoples in the print.
The peoples of the world are grouped as distinct nations, identified through their flags and national costumes.
Christ, saints and angels gaze from the heavens above, symbolising fraternity among the nations of the world.
Sorrieu named the vision the United States of the World, showing how nationalist feelings were spreading across civilised Europe.
Absolutist refers to unrestrained monarchical government, while utopian means an ideal society that is unlikely to actually exist.

keyTerms.meaning: A government or system of rule that has no restraints on the power exercised; typically an unrestrained monarchy.
A vision of a society that is so ideal that it is unlikely to actually exist in reality.
A state in which the majority of its citizens, and not only its rulers, came to develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent.
Personification of freedom in Sorrieu's print, carrying the torch of Enlightenment and the Charter of the Rights of Man.
Sorrieu's utopian dream of all nations living together as democratic and social republics bound by fraternity.
The feeling of brotherhood among the peoples of different nations, symbolised by saints and angels watching from heaven.

sections.trick: Sorrieu 1848 = STOP: Statue of liberty, Torch, Old monarchies smashed, Peoples marching. USA and Switzerland lead because they were already nations.
sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently sets a source based passage on Sorrieu's first print asking about the symbols, and 1 or 3 mark questions on the meaning of absolutist, utopian and nation state.

sections.heading: The French Revolution and the Birth of National Identity
sections.para: The first clear expression of nationalism came with the French Revolution in 1789. France was a full fledged territorial state under an absolute monarch, and the revolution transferred sovereignty from the monarch to the body of French citizens. The revolutionaries proclaimed that it was the people who would henceforth constitute the nation and shape its destiny. Steps were taken to create a sense of collective identity: the ideas of la patrie, the fatherland, and le citoyen, the citizen, emphasised the notion of a united community enjoying equal rights under a constitution. A centralised administrative system was put in place and it formulated uniform laws for all citizens. Internal customs duties and dues were abolished and a uniform system of weights and measures was adopted. Regional dialects were discouraged and French, as it was spoken and written in Paris, became the common language of the nation. The Estates General, elected by citizens, was renamed the National Assembly, a tricolour flag replaced the royal standard, and the Marseillaise composed by Roget de L'Isle became the national anthem. Revolutionary armies carried these ideas abroad into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy in the 1790s.
points: The French Revolution of 1789 transferred sovereignty from the monarch to the body of French citizens, who would shape the destiny of the nation.
The ideas of la patrie, the fatherland, and le citoyen, the citizen, emphasised a community of equal citizens with equal rights under a constitution.
The Estates General, elected by bodies of active citizens, was renamed the National Assembly.
A tricolour flag was chosen to replace the former royal standard of France.
The Marseillaise, composed by Roget de L'Isle, was sung by Marseilles volunteers and later adopted as the national anthem.
A centralised administrative system formulated uniform laws for all citizens, and internal customs duties and dues were abolished.
A uniform system of weights and measures was adopted, and regional dialects were discouraged in favour of standard French.
In the 1790s the Jacobin clubs prepared the way for French armies which carried the idea of nationalism into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy.

keyTerms.meaning: The fatherland; the idea that citizens owe loyalty to the French nation rather than to a king.
The citizen; the notion of a united community enjoying equal rights under a constitution.
The renamed Estates General, elected by active citizens, which claimed the right to make laws for France.
Patriotic hymn composed by Roget de L'Isle, sung by volunteers from Marseilles and adopted as the national anthem of France.
Political clubs in the 1790s whose members prepared the way for French armies and spread nationalism abroad.
Supreme authority within a territory; after 1789 it rested with the French nation and its citizens instead of the king.

sections.trick: 1789 gave France its PATRIOT kit: P for patrie, A for anthem, T for tricolour, R for rights, I for identity, O for one law, T for taxes uniform. Citizens became the nation.
sections.examPointer: Explain any three measures and practices introduced by the French revolutionaries to create a sense of collective identity is a recurring 3 marker, and the tricolour plus Marseillaise are standard MCQs.

sections.heading: Napoleon and the Napoleonic Code of 1804
sections.para: When Napoleon Bonaparte came to power in 1804, he did not destroy the achievements of the revolution but carried them into the lands he conquered. The Civil Code of 1804, usually known as the Napoleonic Code, did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. This code was exported to regions under French control. In the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany, Napoleon simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues. In the towns, guild restrictions were removed. Transport and communication systems were improved, and a uniform decimal system of weights and measures made trade easier. Peasants, artisans, workers and new businessmen enjoyed the new found freedom, and businessmen and small scale producers realised that uniform laws, standardised weights and measures, and a common national currency would facilitate the movement and exchange of goods and capital. Yet in the areas conquered, the reactions of the local populations were mixed. Initially French armies were welcomed as harbingers of liberty, but enthusiasm soon turned to hostility, because increased taxation, censorship, forced conscription into the French armies and the long drawn wars outweighed the administrative changes.
points: The Civil Code of 1804, called the Napoleonic Code, did away with all privileges based on birth and established equality before the law.
The Code secured the right to property and simplified administrative divisions in the regions under French control.
In the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany, Napoleon abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues.
Guild restrictions were removed in towns, which helped traders, artisans and small scale producers.
Transport and communication systems were improved and a uniform decimal system of weights and measures was introduced.
Businessmen realised that uniform laws, standardised weights and a common national currency would facilitate the movement of goods and capital.
French rule was initially welcomed as liberation, but increased taxation, censorship, forced conscription into French armies and long wars turned enthusiasm into hostility.

keyTerms.meaning: The Civil Code of 1804 which established equality before the law, secured the right to property and removed birth privileges across Napoleon's empire.
The medieval system of obligations between lords and peasants; abolished by Napoleon in conquered lands.
The bonded labour of peasants tied to feudal lords, which the Code abolished in territories like the Rhineland.
Payments and services that peasants owed to the lord of the manor, abolished under French rule.
Rules of urban craft associations that controlled production and entry of new producers; removed by Napoleon in towns.
Compulsory military service by which men of conquered regions were forced into the French armies.
A uniform system of weights and measures based on units of ten, introduced to ease trade.

sections.trick: 1804 ERT code: Equality before law, Right to property, Transport and uniform measures. Add the dark side with the word TAXC: Taxation, Administration, X-privileges gone, Censorship and Conscription.
sections.examPointer: Describe any three features of the Napoleonic Code and its impact is a very frequent 3 marker; 5 markers often ask how French rule was both liberating and hated in Europe.

sections.heading: Liberal Nationalism: Political and Economic Dimensions
sections.para: The term liberalism derives from the Latin root liber, meaning free. For the new middle classes liberalism stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law. Politically, it emphasised the concept of government by consent: since the French Revolution, liberalism stood for the end of autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution and representative government through parliament, and the inviolability of private property. Yet equality before the law did not necessarily stand for universal suffrage. In revolutionary France the right to vote and get elected was granted briefly to all men of property, and men without property and all women were excluded from political rights. Economically, liberalism stood for the freedom of markets and the abolition of state imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital. In the German speaking regions, Napoleon's administrative changes had already unified currencies, weights and measures, but a merchant travelling in 1833 from Hamburg to Nuremberg still had to pass through eleven customs barriers and pay a customs duty of about five per cent at each one. The Zollverein, a Prussian led customs union formed in 1834, abolished tariff barriers, reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two, and built a network of railways, laying the economic basis of German nationalism.
points: Liberalism derives from the Latin liber, meaning free, and stood for freedom of the individual and equality of all before the law.
Politically liberals demanded the end of autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution, representative government through parliament and an independent judiciary.
Equality before law did not mean universal suffrage; men without property and all women were excluded from political rights.
Economically liberalism stood for freedom of markets and the abolition of state imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital.
In 1833 a merchant travelling from Hamburg to Nuremberg faced eleven customs barriers and paid about five per cent duty at each one.
Different currencies and measures in more than thirty German states made trade slow, costly and complicated.
The Zollverein of 1834, initiated by Prussia, joined most German states into a customs union that abolished tariff barriers.
The Zollverein reduced currencies from over thirty to two and its railway network knitted the German markets together, preparing economic unity before political unity.

keyTerms.meaning: Ideology of freedom from Latin liber: political freedom through constitutions and parliaments and economic freedom through free markets.
The right of all adult citizens to vote; liberals did not demand it, and women were excluded from political rights.
The right to vote in political elections, restricted in most of Europe to property owning men.
Prussian led customs union of 1834 that abolished tariff barriers and reduced over thirty currencies to two in German states.
A customs duty imposed on goods crossing state borders, which obstructed trade before the Zollverein.
Special rights enjoyed by the Church and its clergy, which liberals wanted to end.
Social group of professionals, businessmen and educated people who became the main carriers of liberal nationalism.

sections.trick: LIBERalism has two faces: one POLITICAL face asking for a Constitution, and one ECONOMIC face asking for open markets. Zollverein 1834 = One Zone, No tariffs, Two currencies, Many railways.
sections.examPointer: Explain the political and economic ideas of liberalism with reference to Zollverein is a standard 5 marker, and the eleven customs barriers story is a favourite source based question.

sections.heading: A New Conservatism after 1815: The Congress of Vienna
sections.para: After Napoleon's defeat in 1815, European governments were driven by a spirit of conservatism. Conservatives believed that established, traditional institutions of state and society, like the monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family, should be preserved. Most conservatives, however, did not propose a return to the pre revolutionary society; they realised that modernisation could strengthen traditional institutions such as a permanent army, an efficient bureaucracy and a dynamic economy. In 1815, representatives of the European powers, Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria, who had collectively defeated Napoleon, met at Vienna to draw up a settlement, and the Congress was hosted by the Austrian Chancellor Metternich. The Bourbon dynasty, deposed during the French Revolution, was restored to power in France, and France lost the territories it had annexed under Napoleon. Belgium was set up with the Netherlands, Genoa was given to Sardinia Piedmont, Austria got control of northern Italy, and Prussia was given part of Saxony and important territories on the Rhine while Russia got part of Poland. The main intention was to restore the monarchies overthrown by Napoleon and create a new conservative order. Conservative regimes imposed censorship: newspapers, books, plays and songs reflecting the ideas of liberty and freedom were controlled, and dissent was punished.
points: Conservatism believed in preserving traditional institutions of state and society such as the monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family.
Most conservatives did not propose a return to pre revolutionary society and accepted that a modern army, bureaucracy and dynamic economy strengthened the state.
The Congress of Vienna was hosted by the Austrian Chancellor Metternich in 1815 with representatives of Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria.
The Bourbon dynasty was restored to power in France, which lost the territories annexed under Napoleon.
Belgium was joined with the Netherlands, Genoa went to Sardinia Piedmont, and Austria got control of northern Italy.
Prussia received part of Saxony and territories on the Rhine, while Russia obtained part of Poland.
The main aim was to undo most changes brought by Napoleon and restore the monarchies overthrown by him, creating a new conservative order.
Conservative regimes imposed censorship laws controlling newspapers, books, plays and songs that carried ideas of liberty and freedom associated with the French Revolution.

keyTerms.meaning: A political philosophy that stressed preservation of traditional institutions like monarchy, Church, property and family.
Settlement drawn up by Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria to undo Napoleonic changes and create a conservative order in Europe.
Austrian Chancellor who hosted the Vienna Congress and became the symbol of the conservative order in Europe.
Royal family of France which was restored to the throne after the defeat of Napoleon.
Official control over newspapers, books, plays and songs to suppress ideas of liberty and nationalism.
Opposition or disagreement with the government, which conservative regimes punished severely.

sections.trick: Vienna 1815 undo map: Bourbon back in France, Belgium with Netherlands, Genoa to Sardinia, North Italy to Austria, Saxony and Rhine to Prussia, Poland chunk to Russia. Remember BRAP: Britain, Russia, Austria, Prussia drew the map.
sections.examPointer: What were the main provisions of the Treaty of Vienna 1815 is a regular 3 or 5 marker; MCQs often test who hosted the Congress and which dynasty was restored.

sections.heading: Secret Societies and the Revolutionaries: Mazzini
sections.para: The fear of repression drove many liberal nationalists underground, and secret societies sprang up in many European states to train revolutionaries and spread their ideas. Revolutionary activities were carried out by the secret societies in most European countries, and their members were usually educated middle class youth, students, professionals and businessmen. Revolutionary opposes the very idea of monarchical government and believes that the nation is the natural unit of mankind, so its existence must be the basis of liberty. The Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Mazzini, born in Genoa in 1805, became a member of the secret society of the Carbonari when he was twenty four. As a young man of twenty four, he was sent into exile in 1831 for attempting a revolution in Liguria. He subsequently founded two more underground societies, first Young Italy in Marseilles and then Young Europe in Berne, whose members were drawn from like minded young men from Poland, France, Italy and the German states. Mazzini believed that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind, so Italy could not continue to be a patchwork of small states and kingdoms; it had to be forged into a single unified republic within a wider alliance of nations. Metternich described Mazzini as the most dangerous enemy of our social order.
points: After 1815 the fear of repression drove liberal nationalists underground, where they formed secret societies to train revolutionaries and spread ideas.
Members of secret societies were largely educated middle class youth, including students, professionals and businessmen who opposed monarchy.
Giuseppe Mazzini was born in Genoa in 1805 and joined the secret society of the Carbonari at the age of twenty four.
Mazzini was sent into exile in 1831 for attempting a revolution in Liguria when he was only twenty four years old.
He founded Young Italy in Marseilles and then Young Europe in Berne, with members from Poland, France, Italy and the German states.
Mazzini believed that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind and that Italy must be unified into a single republic.
His relentless opposition to monarchy and his vision of democratic republics frightened the conservative powers of Europe.
Metternich, the Austrian Chancellor, described Mazzini as the most dangerous enemy of our social order.

keyTerms.meaning: One who opposes monarchical government and believes the nation is the natural unit of mankind and the basis of liberty.
Italian secret society of the early nineteenth century which Mazzini joined at the age of twenty four.
Underground society founded by Mazzini at Marseilles in 1831 to work for a unified Italian republic.
Secret society founded by Mazzini at Berne with members from Poland, France, Italy and the German states.
Italian revolutionary born in Genoa in 1805, exiled in 1831, who became the prophet of Italian nationalism.
Coastal region of Italy where Mazzini attempted a revolution in 1831, for which he was exiled.

sections.trick: Mazzini timeline: 1805 born, 24 joins Carbonari, 1831 exile, then Young Italy plus Young Europe. Remember MYE: Mazzini, Young Italy, Young Europe.
sections.examPointer: Who was Mazzini and what was his contribution, and why did Metternich call him dangerous, appear as 3 markers; his birth year 1805 and exile 1831 are repeated MCQs.

sections.heading: The Revolutions of 1830: France, Belgium and Greece
sections.para: The decade of the 1830s saw a wave of revolution sweep Europe. In July 1830 the Bourbon king Charles X was overthrown by liberals, who installed a constitutional monarchy under Louis Philippe. Metternich remarked that when France sneezes, the whole of Europe catches cold, and indeed the July Revolution sparked an uprising in Brussels that led to Belgium breaking away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. An event that mobilised nationalist feelings among the educated elite across Europe was the Greek War of Independence, which began in 1821. Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century, and the growth of revolutionary nationalism in Europe sparked off a struggle for independence. Support poured in from Greeks living in exile and also from many West Europeans who sympathised with the ancient Greek culture and lauded it as the cradle of European civilisation. The English poet Lord Byron mobilised funds and went to fight in the war, where he died of fever in 1824. Finally, with the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832, Greece was recognised as an independent nation. The revolutionaries of this decade also included the Polish struggle, where a revolt against Russian rule broke out.
points: In July 1830 the Bourbon king Charles X was overthrown and Louis Philippe was installed as a constitutional monarch in France.
Metternich remarked that when France sneezes, the whole of Europe catches cold, showing how revolutionary events spread across Europe.
The July Revolution sparked an uprising in Brussels which led to Belgium breaking away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
The Greek War of Independence began in 1821 and mobilised nationalist feelings among the educated elite across Europe.
Greece had been part of the Ottoman Empire since the fifteenth century before its independence struggle began.
Greeks living in exile and West Europeans who saw Greece as the cradle of European civilisation supported the struggle.
The English poet Lord Byron mobilised funds for the Greek cause and went to fight, dying of fever in 1824.
The Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation.

keyTerms.meaning: Bourbon king of France overthrown by the July Revolution of 1830.
Constitutional monarch installed in France after the 1830 revolution.
Struggle begun in 1821 against Ottoman rule, supported by exiled Greeks and West European sympathisers.
English poet who raised funds and fought for Greek independence, dying of fever in 1824.
Agreement that recognised Greece as an independent nation.
Turkish empire which had ruled Greece since the fifteenth century and later ruled the Balkans.

sections.trick: 1830 chain reaction: Charles out, Louis Philippe in, Belgium breaks free, Greece fights on. Sneeze rule: France sneezes, Europe catches cold. Greece gets freedom by Constantinople 1832.
sections.examPointer: The Metternich sneeze quote is a favourite MCQ; short questions on the Greek War of Independence, Byron and the Treaty of Constantinople 1832 appear regularly.

sections.heading: 1848: The Revolution of the Liberals and the Frankfurt Parliament
sections.para: Food shortage and widespread unemployment in Europe brought the population of Paris out on the roads in 1848. Barricades were erected and Louis Philippe was forced to flee, and a National Assembly proclaimed a Republic, granted suffrage to all males above twenty one and guaranteed the right to work, with national workshops set up to provide employment. Earlier, in 1845, weavers in Silesia had led a revolt against contractors who supplied them raw material and gave them orders for finished goods but drastically reduced their payments. In the German regions a large number of political associations, mainly of middle class professionals, businessmen and prosperous artisans, came together in Frankfurt and decided to vote for an all German National Assembly. On 18 May 1848, 831 elected representatives marched in a festive procession to take their places in the Frankfurt Parliament convened in the Church of St Paul, and they drafted a constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament. When the crown was offered to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, he rejected it and joined the monarchs and the military in opposing the elected assembly. The social basis of the parliament eroded, women were present only as spectators, and troops forced the assembly to disband. However, the monarchs had realised that the cycle of revolution and repression could only be ended by granting concessions, so serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg dominions and in Russia.
points: Food shortage and widespread unemployment brought the population of Paris out on the roads and barricades were erected in 1848.
Louis Philippe fled and a National Assembly proclaimed a Republic, granted suffrage to all men above twenty one and guaranteed the right to work.
In 1845 weavers in Silesia led a revolt against contractors who supplied raw material and took finished cloth but drastically reduced their payments.
The Frankfurt Parliament, with 831 elected representatives, convened on 18 May 1848 in the Church of St Paul in Frankfurt.
The parliament drafted a constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament.
When the crown was offered to Friedrich Wilhelm IV of Prussia, he rejected it and joined other monarchs and the military in opposing the assembly.
Women were present only as spectators in the Frankfurt Parliament while men of the middle classes dominated the proceedings.
After 1848 monarchs realised that repression had to be balanced with concessions, and serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg dominions and in Russia.

keyTerms.meaning: All German National Assembly of 831 members that met in St Paul's Church in 1848 and drafted a constitution for Germany.
King of Prussia who refused the crown of a united Germany offered by the Frankfurt Parliament.
The right to vote; granted to all adult males above twenty one in France after the 1848 revolution.
Employment schemes set up in France in 1848 to guarantee the right to work.
Uprising of 1845 by Silesian weavers against contractors who drastically reduced their payments.
Form of government without a monarch, proclaimed in France in 1848 by the National Assembly.
A right or privilege granted by rulers to calm revolutionary pressure, such as the abolition of serfdom after 1848.

sections.trick: 1848 double revolution: Paris got a Republic plus Right to work; Frankfurt got 831 men, one crown refused, zero result. Remember 18 May and St Paul's Church.
sections.examPointer: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail is one of the most repeated 3 markers in CBSE boards, and the Silesian weavers' revolt and French measures of 1848 appear in 5 markers.

sections.heading: Romanticism, Folk Culture and Language as Nationalism
sections.para: Nationalism did not spread only through wars and parliaments; culture, including music, stories, art and poetry, played a vital role in shaping nationalist feelings. Romantic artists and poets generally criticised the glorification of reason and science, and instead focused on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings. Their effort was to create a sense of a shared collective heritage, a common cultural past, as the basis of a nation. The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people, das volk, and the essence of the nation was expressed through its volksgeist or spirit of the people; folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances were therefore collected and recorded. The Grimm brothers compiled German folk tales, and collecting folklore became a way of carrying the modern nationalist message to large audiences who were mostly illiterate. In Poland, which had been partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria and had lost independent political existence, language became a weapon of national resistance. The Polish clergy used Polish for religious instruction even after the Russian government imposed the Russian language everywhere, and after the Polish uprising of 1831 was crushed, many priests and bishops were jailed or exiled. The composer Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through his operas and music, turning folk dances like the polonaise and the mazurka into nationalist symbols.
points: Romantic artists and poets criticised the glorification of reason and science and emphasised emotions, intuition and mystical feelings.
Culture in the form of art, poetry, stories and music helped create and express nationalist feelings across Europe.
Romanticism sought to develop a particular form of nationalist sentiment by creating a sense of a shared collective heritage and common cultural past.
Johann Gottfried Herder claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people, das volk, expressed through the volksgeist.
Folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances were collected and recorded because the true spirit of the nation lived among ordinary people.
Collecting and recording folklore was not merely to recover an ancient spirit but to carry the modern nationalist message to mostly illiterate people.
In partitioned Poland, the Polish language became a weapon of national resistance, and the clergy used it for religious instruction against Russian bans.
After the 1831 Polish uprising was crushed, Russian was imposed and Polish forced out of schools, and Karol Kurpinski turned the polonaise and mazurka into nationalist symbols.

keyTerms.meaning: Cultural movement that emphasised emotions, intuition and mystical feelings rather than reason, and built national sentiment through art and folklore.
The common people among whom, according to Herder, the true culture of the nation was to be discovered.
The spirit of the people, the essence of the nation expressed through its language, songs and traditions.
German philosopher who argued that folk culture, not elites, carried the true spirit of the nation.
The German word for the common folk of the nation whose traditions romanticists collected.
Polish composer who celebrated the national struggle through operas and turned folk dances into nationalist symbols.
Polish folk dances which Kurpinski transformed into symbols of national resistance.
The local mother tongue, such as Polish, used as a weapon of national resistance against imposed foreign languages.

sections.trick: Culture sings what swords cannot say: Herder hunted das volk, Grimm gathered tales, Kurpinski danced the polonaise and mazurka, and Poland prayed in Polish. Remember the chain HERD to GRIMM to KURP.
sections.examPointer: How did culture and language help develop nationalist feelings, with reference to Poland and Herder, is a frequent 5 marker; das volk and folk culture are common 1 and 3 markers.

sections.heading: The Unification of Germany
sections.para: After 1848 nationalist sentiment in Europe moved away from its association with democracy and revolution, and conservative forces were able to harness it to their own political ends. Nationalist feelings were widespread among middle class Germans, who in 1848 had tried to unite the different regions into a nation state governed by an elected parliament, but this liberal initiative was repressed by the combined forces of the monarchy and the military, supported by the large landowners called Junkers of Prussia. Prussia now took on the leadership of the movement for national unification, and its chief minister, Otto von Bismarck, was the architect of this process, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy. Three wars over seven years, with Austria, Denmark and France, ended in Prussian victory and completed the process of unification. In January 1871, the Prussian king, William I, was proclaimed German Emperor, an event held with great pomp at Versailles, on a note of triumph for the Prussian army's victories. The new German state stressed its modernising character: the currency, banking, legal and judicial systems in Germany were modernised and standardised. The unification demonstrated the dominance of Prussian state power, and the nation was built from above by iron and bureaucracy rather than by liberal parliamentarians.
points: After 1848 nationalist sentiment moved away from democracy and revolution, and conservative forces harnessed nationalism for their own ends.
The liberal initiative of unification was repressed by the monarchy, the military and the large landowners of Prussia called Junkers.
Prussia took over the leadership of the movement for national unification after the failure of the Frankfurt Parliament.
Otto von Bismarck, chief minister of Prussia, was the architect of unification, carried out with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
Three wars over seven years with Austria, Denmark and France ended in Prussian victory and completed unification.
In January 1871 the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor in a ceremony held at Versailles.
The proclamation at Versailles displayed Prussian power and Prussian measures and currency became the standard in Germany.
The new German empire modernised its currency, banking, legal and judicial systems, and unification was achieved from above, not by liberal democracy.

keyTerms.meaning: Chief minister of Prussia and architect of German unification through three wars and diplomacy with army and bureaucracy.
Prussian king proclaimed German Emperor in January 1871 at Versailles.
Large landowners of Prussia who supported the monarchy and military against liberal parliamentarians.
Leading German state whose army and bureaucracy unified Germany in 1871.
Palace in France where William I was proclaimed German Emperor in January 1871.
Bismarck's policy of achieving unification through military power and war rather than speeches and parliaments.

sections.trick: Bismarck's three wars in order: Denmark first, Austria second, France last. Remember DAF 64, 66, 71: Denmark 1864, Austria 1866, France 1870 to 71, crowned January 1871 at Versailles.
sections.examPointer: Describe the role of Bismarck and the process of German unification is a favourite 5 marker; MCQs test the years of the three wars and the proclamation at Versailles in January 1871.

sections.heading: The Unification of Italy and the Making of Britain
sections.para: Italy had a long history of political fragmentation: Italians were scattered over several dynastic states as well as the multi national Habsburg Empire. During the middle of the nineteenth century Italy was divided into seven states, of which only one, Sardinia Piedmont, was ruled by an Italian princely house; the north was under Austrian Habsburgs, the centre was ruled by the Pope, and the southern regions were under the domination of the Bourbon kings of Spain. The Italian language had still not acquired one common form, and Mazzini's programmes of the 1830s and 1840s for a unitary Italian Republic had failed to inspire. The failure of the revolutionary uprisings of 1831 and 1848 meant that the mantle of leading Italian unification now fell on Sardinia Piedmont under its ruler Victor Emmanuel II. In a diplomatic move, Chief Minister Cavour, who spoke French much better than Italian, secured a secret alliance with France in 1859 which enabled Sardinia Piedmont to defeat Austria. In 1860 Garibaldi marched to southern Italy with his armed volunteers called the Red Shirts, won the support of local peasants and drove out the Spanish rulers of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of united Italy, and Rome was captured later when the Franco Prussian War broke out in 1870. Unlike Germany and Italy, Britain was a nation state long before: the Act of Union of 1707 united England and Scotland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain, and Ireland was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom in 1801.
points: In the mid nineteenth century Italy was divided into seven states, with Sardinia Piedmont the only one ruled by an Italian princely house.
Northern Italy was under the Austrian Habsburgs, the centre was ruled by the Pope, and the south was ruled by the Bourbon kings of Spain.
The Italian language had not yet acquired a single common form, and only a small percentage of the population spoke standard Italian.
Mazzini's efforts in the 1830s and 1840s to create a unitary Italian Republic failed to inspire the Italians.

Britain became a nation state gradually: the Act of Union of 1707 united England and Scotland, and Ireland was forcibly incorporated in 1801.

sections.heading: Visualising the Nation and the Balkan Powder Keg
sections.para: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries artists personified a nation, giving the abstract idea a concrete form. Nations were portrayed as female figures, chosen to personify the nation did not stand for any particular woman in real life; rather it sought to give the abstract idea of the nation a concrete form. In France the female figure was named Marianne, a popular Christian name, which underlined the idea of a people's nation; her characteristics were drawn from Liberty and the Republic, with the red cap, the tricolour and the cockade. Statues of Marianne were erected in public squares and her images were marked on coins and stamps to remind the public of the national symbol of unity. Germania became the allegory of the German nation; she wears a crown of oak leaves, since the German oak stands for heroism. In the Balkans, meanwhile, nationalism took an explosive turn. The region, comprising modern day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, had inhabitants broadly known as Slavs, and a large part was under the control of the weakening Ottoman Empire. The spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism and the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made this region very explosive: one by one its European subject nationalities broke free and declared independence, using history as evidence of former independence. Intense rivalry among the European powers over trade, colonies, and naval and military might turned the Balkans into a scene of big power conflict, with the Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913 and finally the assassination at Sarajevo in June 1914 igniting the First World War.
points: Artists in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries personified the nation as female figures to give the abstract idea of a nation a concrete form.
Marianne, the allegory of France, was characterised by the red cap, the tricolour and the cockade, drawn from Liberty and the Republic.
Statues of Marianne were erected in public squares and her images were marked on coins and stamps as a national symbol of unity.
Germania, the allegory of Germany, wears a crown of oak leaves because the German oak stands for heroism.
The Balkans comprised modern Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, inhabited largely by Slavs.
Romantic nationalism and the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire made the Balkans explosive, as subject nationalities broke away one by one claiming independence.
The big European powers, Russia, Germany, England and Austro Hungary, competed over trade, colonies and naval and military might, making the Balkans a scene of rivalry.
The Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 and the Sarajevo assassination of June 1914 finally led to the First World War.

boardQuestions.question: What is a nation state? How did it differ from the dynastic states of Europe?
boardQuestions.answer: A nation state is a state in which the majority of its citizens, and not only its rulers, came to develop a sense of common identity, often shared history and descent. Unlike dynastic states ruled by hereditary kings over scattered territories, its citizens identify with the nation itself.

boardQuestions.question: Describe any three features of the Napoleonic Code of 1804.
boardQuestions.answer: The Civil Code of 1804, called the Napoleonic Code, carried the achievements of the French Revolution into conquered Europe. 1) It did away with all privileges based on birth and established equality before the law for every citizen. 2) It secured the right to property, giving legal protection to owners of land and capital. 3) It simplified administrative divisions and applied uniform laws across the regions under French control. In addition, it freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, removed guild restrictions in towns, improved transport and communication and introduced a uniform decimal system of weights and measures, all of which helped trade. However, increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription into the French armies soon turned the initial enthusiasm of the conquered peoples into hostility.

boardQuestions.question: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail in its mission of unifying Germany?
boardQuestions.answer: The Frankfurt Parliament, which met in the Church of St Paul on 18 May 1848 with 831 elected representatives, drafted a constitution for a German nation headed by a monarchy subject to parliament. It failed for the following reasons. 1) Lack of mass support: the assembly was dominated by middle class professionals, businessmen and prosperous artisans, and it lacked the support of workers, peasants and artisans. 2) Royal opposition: when the crown was offered to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, King of Prussia, he rejected it, and the monarchs, the military and the large landowners called Junkers strengthened their position against the parliamentarians. 3) Internal weakness: the social basis of the parliament eroded with time and women, who had raised their voice, remained only spectators. In the end troops were called in and the parliament was forced to disband, showing that liberal hopes of unification through an elected body had collapsed.

boardQuestions.question: Explain any three consequences of the Treaty of Vienna 1815.
boardQuestions.answer: The Congress of Vienna, hosted by Metternich in 1815, undid most of the changes that had come about in Europe during the Napoleonic wars. 1) The Bourbon dynasty, which had been deposed during the French Revolution, was restored to power in France, and France lost the territories it had annexed under Napoleon. 2) Territorial reshuffling took place: Belgium was set up with the Netherlands, Genoa was given to Sardinia Piedmont, Austria gained control of northern Italy, and Prussia received part of Saxony and territories on the Rhine while Russia obtained part of Poland. 3) A new conservative order was created in which autocratic powers of the monarchies were strengthened, and censorship laws were imposed to control newspapers, books, plays and songs carrying ideas of liberty and freedom.

boardQuestions.question: Who was Giuseppe Mazzini? Describe his contribution to Italian nationalism.
boardQuestions.answer: Giuseppe Mazzini was an Italian revolutionary, born in Genoa in 1805, who became a member of the secret society of the Carbonari at the age of twenty four. Contribution: 1) He was sent into exile in 1831 for attempting a revolution in Liguria, and he then founded two underground societies, Young Italy in Marseilles and Young Europe in Berne, whose members came from Poland, France, Italy and the German states. 2) He firmly believed that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind, and therefore Italy could not continue to be a patchwork of small states; it had to be forged into a single unified republic. 3) His relentless opposition to monarchy and his vision of democratic republics so frightened conservative regimes that Metternich described him as the most dangerous enemy of our social order. His ideas inspired the later unification achieved by Cavour and Garibaldi.

boardQuestions.question: How did the female allegory represent nations? Explain with reference to Marianne and Germania.
boardQuestions.answer: Artists in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries personified the nation so that the abstract idea of a nation could be given a concrete form; the female figure chosen did not stand for any particular woman in real life. In France the figure was named Marianne, a popular Christian name which underlined the idea of a people's nation. Her characteristics were drawn from Liberty and the Republic, marked by the red cap, the tricolour and the cockade, and statues of Marianne were erected in public squares while her images were marked on coins and stamps to remind people of the national symbol of unity. In Germany the allegory was Germania, who wears a crown of oak leaves, because the German oak stands for heroism. Such images helped ordinary people emotionally identify with the nation and turned nationalism into a living symbol.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the process of the unification of Germany.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: In 1848 middle class Germans had tried to unite the different German regions into a nation state governed by an elected parliament, but the liberal initiative of the Frankfurt Parliament was crushed by the monarchy, the military and the Junkers of Prussia. After this failure, the mantle of leading the nation fell on Prussia. Body: 1) Leadership: Prussia took on the leadership of the movement for national unification, and its Chief Minister, Otto von Bismarck, became the architect of the process, which was carried out with the help of the Prussian army and the bureaucracy rather than through any popular parliament. 2) Wars: Bismarck fought three wars over seven years, first against Denmark in 1864, then against Austria in 1866 and finally against France in 1870 to 1871. Each ended in Prussian victory and each step brought more German states under Prussian leadership, completing the process of unification. 3) Proclamation: In January 1871 the Prussian king, William I, was proclaimed German Emperor at a ceremony held at Versailles, on a note of triumph for the Prussian army's victories. The event demonstrated the dominance of Prussian state power, and many joined the proclamation out of respect for Prussian victory rather than democratic choice. 4) Modernisation: The new German state stressed its modernising character by unifying the currency, banking, legal and judicial systems of Germany, and Prussian measures and currency became the general standard for the whole empire. Conclusion: Thus German unification was achieved from above, through blood and iron, in which nationalism was harnessed by conservative forces to strengthen the Prussian monarchy rather than to create a liberal democracy.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the role of Cavour and Garibaldi in the unification of Italy.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: In the mid nineteenth century Italy was divided into seven states, of which only Sardinia Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house, while the north was under Austria, the centre under the Pope and the south under the Bourbon kings of Spain. Mazzini's earlier revolutionary efforts had failed, so the task of unification fell on Sardinia Piedmont under Victor Emmanuel II. Body: 1) Role of Cavour: Count Cavour, the Chief Minister of Sardinia Piedmont, was the architect of Italian unification through diplomacy. He understood that Sardinia could not defeat Austria alone, so he secured a secret alliance with France, and in the war of 1859 Sardinia Piedmont, with French help, succeeded in defeating Austria and freeing northern Italy from Habsburg control. Interestingly, Cavour spoke French much better than Italian, showing how the Italian elites themselves were culturally divided. 2) Role of Garibaldi: In 1860 Garibaldi, a supporter of Mazzini, marched to southern Italy with his armed volunteers known as the Red Shirts. He won the support of the local peasants and drove out the Spanish rulers, conquering the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. His southern campaign united the north and the south of the peninsula. In 1867 he again led volunteers towards Rome, and Rome was finally captured in 1870 when French troops withdrew during the Franco Prussian War. Conclusion: In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of united Italy, and the long dream of Mazzini was realised largely through the diplomacy of Cavour and the sword of Garibaldi, though not all inhabitants of the new kingdom spoke Italian or shared one culture.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the political and economic ideas of liberalism in nineteenth century Europe.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: The term liberalism derives from the Latin root liber, meaning free, and for the new middle classes it stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law. Body: 1) Political ideas: Politically, liberalism emphasised the concept of government by consent. Since the French Revolution, liberalism stood for the end of autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution and representative government through parliament, and the inviolability of private property. It also stressed an independent judiciary so that laws could not be twisted by rulers. 2) Limits of liberal equality: Equality before the law did not necessarily stand for universal suffrage. In revolutionary France the right to vote and to get elected was granted briefly to all men of property, but men without property and all women were excluded from political rights, and women were present only as spectators in public political life. 3) Economic ideas: In the economic sphere, liberalism stood for the freedom of markets and the abolition of state imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital. In the German speaking regions, a merchant travelling in 1833 from Hamburg to Nuremberg to sell goods had to pass through eleven customs barriers and pay a customs duty of about five per cent at each one, and duties were often greater than the price of the goods. Currencies and measures differed from state to state, making trade slow and costly. 4) Zollverein: The Prussian led customs union, the Zollverein, formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia, joined many German states, abolished tariff barriers and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two, and its railway network carried goods and people freely. Conclusion: Thus liberal nationalism joined political freedom with economic unity, and the economic unification achieved by the Zollverein prepared the ground for the political unification of Germany in 1871.

boardQuestions.question: Describe the revolutions of 1848 in France and Germany. What changes did monarchs accept after these revolutions?
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: The year 1848 saw simultaneous revolutions in France and the German regions, driven by food shortage, unemployment and demands for political rights. Body: 1) Revolution in France: Food shortage and widespread unemployment brought the population of Paris out on the roads, barricades were erected and King Louis Philippe was forced to flee. A National Assembly proclaimed a Republic, granted suffrage to all males above twenty one and guaranteed the right to work, and national workshops were set up to provide employment to the jobless. 2) Revolution in Germany: Men and women of the liberal middle classes combined demands for constitutionalism with national unification. Political associations of middle class professionals, businessmen and prosperous artisans came together in Frankfurt and voted for an all German National Assembly. On 18 May 1848, 831 elected representatives met in the Church of St Paul, drafted a constitution for a German nation headed by a monarchy subject to parliament, and offered the crown to Friedrich Wilhelm IV, who refused it. The assembly was finally dispersed by troops. 3) Failure and concessions: The Frankfurt Parliament failed because it lacked mass support, monarchs opposed it and women remained spectators. Yet the monarchs realised that the cycle of revolution and repression could only be ended by granting concessions. After 1848 serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg dominions and in Russia, and the Habsburg rulers granted more autonomy to the Hungarians in 1867. Conclusion: The revolutions of 1848 showed that liberal demands for constitutional government and national unification could no longer be ignored, even though they failed in their immediate aims.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract: 'In 1848, Frédéric Sorrieu, a French artist, prepared a series of four prints visualising his dream of a world made up of democratic and social republics. The peoples of the world are grouped as distinct nations, identified through their flags and national costumes.' Answer: (a) What do the shattered remains in the foreground symbolise? (b) Which two countries lead the procession and why? (c) What is a utopian vision?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) The shattered remains of the symbols of absolutist institutions lie in the foreground of the print, symbolising the end of unrestrained monarchical rule and the defeat of absolute monarchies by liberty. (b) The United States and Switzerland lead the procession because by 1848 they were already nation states, the United States having survived a civil war to forge a federal state and Switzerland being constituted as a nation through a treaty of unified provinces. (c) Utopian means a vision of a society that is so ideal that it is unlikely to actually exist; Sorrieu's dream of a United States of the World, where all peoples lived as democratic and social republics bound by fraternity, was such a utopian vision. The passage shows how nationalist imagination had become a European mood even before most nations existed.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract: 'The most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871 was the area called the Balkans. The spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism made this region very explosive.' Answer: (a) Which empire controlled the Balkans? (b) Why did the Balkan nationalities seek independence? (c) How did the Balkan crisis lead to the First World War?
boardQuestions.answer: (a) A large part of the Balkans was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, which by the late nineteenth century was disintegrating under internal weakness and nationalist pressure. (b) The inhabitants were broadly known as Slavs, and the spread of romantic nationalism made the peoples of the region identify themselves on the basis of nationality and shared history; each nationality claimed independence using history to prove that they had once been independent, so jealousy and rivalry developed among the Balkan states themselves. (c) The Balkans became an area of intense rivalry among the big European powers, Russia, Germany, England and Austro Hungary, each of which hoped to gain trade, colonies and naval and military strength there. The Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 created further tension, and the Sarajevo assassination of June 1914 ignited the First World War, showing how nationalism aligned with imperialism turned Europe into a war zone.

boardQuestions.question: 'Nationalism, aligned with imperialism, led Europe to disaster in 1914.' Explain the role of the Balkans in this statement.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: After 1871, the most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe was the area called the Balkans, a region of geographical and ethnic variation comprising modern day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as the Slavs. Body: 1) Ottoman decline: A large part of the Balkans was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, and the disintegration of this empire, combined with the spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism, made the region very explosive. 2) Balkan nationalism: One by one, the European subject nationalities of the Balkans broke free from Ottoman control and declared independence. They used history to prove that they had once been independent and therefore had the right to freedom, but at the same time the Balkan peoples became intensely jealous of one another and each state hoped to gain more territory at the expense of its neighbours. 3) Big power rivalry: During this period there was intense rivalry among the European powers over trade and colonies as well as naval and military might. The Balkans became the scene of big power rivalry, with Russia, Germany, England and Austro Hungary each hoping to gain control. This turned the region into one of perpetual conflict and war. 4) The slide to war: The Balkan Wars of 1912 and 1913 added to the tension, and the assassination of the Austrian Archduke at Sarajevo in June 1914 triggered the First World War, in which nationalism was aligned with imperialism. Conclusion: Thus the ideal of democratic nationhood, when it mixed with imperial ambition in the Balkans, did not bring freedom and peace but prepared Europe for disaster in 1914.

boardQuestions.question: How did romanticism and folk culture help in the growth of nationalism in Europe? Explain with examples of Germany and Poland.
boardQuestions.answer: Introduction: Nationalism spread through culture as much as through wars and parliaments, and romanticism, a cultural movement, played a vital role in shaping nationalist feelings. Body: 1) Romantic ideas: Romantic artists and poets generally criticised the glorification of reason and science and focused instead on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings. Their effort was to create a sense of a shared collective heritage, a common cultural past, as the basis of a nation. 2) Germany and folk culture: The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people, das volk, and that the essence of the nation was expressed through its volksgeist, or spirit of the people. Folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances were collected and recorded, and the Grimm brothers compiled German folk tales; collecting folklore was meant to carry the modern nationalist message to large audiences who were mostly illiterate. 3) Poland and language: Poland, partitioned by Russia, Prussia and Austria, had no independent political existence, yet national feelings were kept alive through music and language. Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through operas and music, turning folk dances like the polonaise and mazurka into nationalist symbols. After the Polish uprising of 1831 was crushed, the Russian language was imposed everywhere, but the Polish clergy continued to use Polish for religious instruction, and many priests and bishops were jailed or exiled. The use of Polish itself became a symbol of the struggle against Russian domination. Conclusion: Thus romanticism, folklore and vernacular language gave nations a cultural soul, and where political freedom was absent, as in Poland, culture itself became the weapon of nationalism.
